title: Your TMP36 code, value = 153. What does this print?
explain: value * 5 / 1023 is all int: 765 / 1023 = 0, and the float comes too late. In value * 5.0 the first step is already double, so the division keeps the fraction. One floating operand in the FIRST operation is enough.

title: Arduino Uno, int is 16-bit (int16_t here). What does this print?
explain: 1023 * 5000 = 5 115 000 does not fit in 16 bits (max 32 767). Only the low 16 bits stay: 5 115 000 mod 65 536 = 3 192. No warning, just a wrong number. 5000L makes the multiplication long (32-bit), and it fits.

title: millis() just wrapped. What does current - previous give?
explain: unsigned long is 32-bit, arithmetic modulo 2^32. The subtraction 'jumps' over zero correctly: 496 ms passed. That is why current - previous >= interval works after 49.7 days.

title: Works for a month, then the LED stops blinking on day 50. Tap the bug.
explain: Near the wrap, previous + interval overflows to a small number, or millis() wraps to a small number while previous + interval is huge: the comparison is wrong. Compare the elapsed time instead: the subtraction is correct across the wrap.

title: mV = 1045. Printing volts like in your first try. Output?
explain: 1045 % 1000 = 45, and printing 45 gives '45', not '045'. A number does not know it is 'after the point'. Pad it: if (mv < 100) print '0'; if (mv < 10) print '0' — or printf("%03ld").

title: temp_x10 = -5 means -0.5 °C. Printing it this way gives?
explain: -5 / 10 = 0 in C (rounds toward zero), and 0 has no sign: the minus is lost. Your final code printed the sign separately and first, then used the absolute value. Always test edge cases: 0, just below 0, just above.

title: TMP36 on a 10-bit ADC with 5 V reference. Smallest step you can see?
explain: One ADC step = 5 V / 1024 ≈ 4.9 mV, and TMP36 gives 10 mV per °C, so one step ≈ 0.49 °C. Printing 0.1 °C shows more digits (precision) than the sensor can resolve (resolution), and accuracy (±1–2 °C) is worse still.

title: Resolution, precision, accuracy (your TMP36 lesson)
bullets: Resolution: the smallest change you can see. 10-bit ADC at 5 V ≈ 4.9 mV ≈ 0.49 °C.
Precision: how many digits you show, or how close repeated readings are. 25.3 °C has 0.1 °C digits.
Accuracy: how close the reading is to the real temperature. TMP36 is about ±1–2 °C.
More digits do not make a better measurement. Print what the hardware can really resolve.

title: Night light with one threshold (LED on when LDR value < 300). At dusk the LED flickers. Fix?
options: Two thresholds: on below 300, off above 350
explain: Near the threshold, noise moves the value up and down across 300, so the LED toggles. Hysteresis uses two levels with a gap: once on, it stays on until the value is clearly higher. Same idea as a Schmitt trigger.

title: 9 V battery, R1 = 10 kΩ on top, R2 = 4.7 kΩ to ground. Vout?
explain: Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2) = 9 × 4.7 / 14.7 ≈ 2.88 V. Check: R2 is about one third of the total, so Vout is about one third of 9 V. Your open practice tasks 2–10 are the same formula with other values.

title: You want to measure the LED current with the multimeter in A mode. How do you connect it?
options: In series: break the circuit and put the meter in the path
explain: In A mode the meter is almost a wire (very low resistance). In series, all current flows through it. In parallel, or between 5 V and GND, it makes a short circuit: big current, blown fuse.

title: Your 74HC00 does nothing. The chip sits fully on one side of the breadboard. Why?
options: Each column of 5 holes is connected: pins on the same column are shorted
Breadboards do not work with chips
explain: The holes in one short column are connected inside. A chip must straddle the center gap, so pin 1 and pin 14 (and every opposite pair) are on different columns. Otherwise opposite pins are shorted.

title: One press should count once, but the counter jumps by hundreds. Tap the bug.
explain: This counts every loop() while the button is held: thousands per second. Count the edge: pressed now AND not pressed last time. Then add debounce, because the contacts bounce for a few ms.

title: Your Reset_Handler calls main with bl, and there is no loop after it. main returns. What happens?
options: The CPU runs the next bytes in flash
explain: main returns into Reset_Handler (bl saved the address in lr). Then Reset_Handler itself returns, but nobody called it: at reset lr is 0xFFFFFFFF. Jumping there is invalid → HardFault. Predictable, but still a crash. That is why startup code ends with b . (an endless loop).

title: What does bl main write into lr (R14)?
options: The address of the next instruction after bl (the return address)
explain: bl = branch with link: lr = return address, then jump. bx lr or pop {…, pc} returns. A function that calls others saves lr on the stack first, because each bl overwrites it.

title: You forgot the .data copy. int counter = 5; still reads 5 after pressing reset. Why is this dangerous?
options: It is not: the bug is impossible
RAM keeps the last value across a reset: it fails only after a real power cycle
Flash and RAM are the same memory
explain: Reset does not clear SRAM. The 5 from your last run is still there, so the bug hides. After power-off, RAM holds random bits and counter is garbage. Test startup code with a real power cycle.

title: Where do these live at run time? const int table[4] = {…}; int counter = 5; static int hits;
options: table: flash (.rodata) · counter: SRAM, start value copied from flash (.data) · hits: SRAM, zeroed (.bss)
table: SRAM · counter: flash · hits: flash
explain: .rodata stays in flash. .data needs a start value, so the value is stored in flash and the startup code copies it to RAM. .bss has no stored value: startup code fills it with zeros.

title: You build with --gc-sections. Why does the vector table section need KEEP(*(.isr_vector))?
options: No code references it, so the linker would remove it as 'unused' → no reset vector
explain: --gc-sections removes sections that nothing references. The CPU reads the vector table by address at reset; no C code uses it. KEEP tells the linker it must stay.

title: Your first GPIO_Init. Someone passes PinNumber = 16. Tap the first line that goes wrong.
explain: With pin 16, 2 * pin = 32: shifting a 32-bit value by 32 is undefined behavior, and each 2-bit field lands outside the register. Check arguments first and return an error, like your fixed version does.

title: SYSCFG_PCLK_EN() and on the very next line you read SYSCFG->EXTICR. What can go wrong on STM32F4?
options: The clock is not active yet for a few cycles: the access can be lost (errata). Read the enable register back first
explain: The errata sheet says a peripheral access right after enabling its clock can fail. ST's HAL does a dummy read-back of the RCC enable register, which waits until the write is done. Your *_PCLK_EN() macros do that now.

title: In gpio::init, why clear gpio_oe and gpio_out BEFORE switching FUNCSEL to SIO?
options: So the pin cannot drive an old, random level for a moment when SIO takes it over
FUNCSEL needs OE = 0 to accept the write
explain: When the pin switches to SIO, SIO's output enable and output value apply at once. Clearing them first means the pin starts as an input with a known level. Clearing ISO last connects the pad only when all is set.

title: auto& sio = at<SioRegs>(addr::kSio); What does this do?
options: Treats the memory at 0xd0000000 as a SioRegs struct and returns a reference to it
explain: reinterpret_cast turns the number into a pointer; *p gives a reference. Nothing is allocated: the registers already live there. static_assert(offsetof(...)) checks that each struct field sits at the real register offset.

title: make builds fine, but in Zed 'go to definition' on cfg->OutputLevel does nothing. Most likely cause?
options: clangd does not know the include paths: no compile_commands.json / compile_flags.txt
explain: The Makefile passes -Idrivers/Inc to the compiler, but clangd reads its own config. Give it compile_commands.json (CMake/bear) or compile_flags.txt, and --query-driver for the ARM toolchain headers.
